title: Binary Search
tagline: Halve the search space every step — find anything sorted in O(log n).

intuition.analogy: Think of looking up a word in a paper dictionary. You don't start at page 1 — you flip to the middle, see whether your word comes before or after, and throw away half the dictionary. Repeat until one page is left. That's binary search.
paragraphs: Binary search answers one question incredibly fast: 'where is X in this sorted list?' The magic comes from the data being sorted. Because everything to the left of any position is smaller and everything to the right is larger, a single comparison at the middle tells you which half can possibly contain your target — and lets you discard the other half entirely.

Each step throws away half of what's left. Starting with n elements you go n → n/2 → n/4 → ... → 1. The number of halvings needed is log₂(n). For a million elements that's about 20 steps. For a billion, only 30. That's the whole reason binary search feels almost magical.

The hard part isn't the idea — it's the bookkeeping. Getting the boundaries (lo, hi), the loop condition, and the mid update exactly right is where most bugs live. Once you internalise the invariant 'the answer, if it exists, is always inside [lo, hi]', the details fall into place.
intuition.keyIdea: If the data is sorted, one comparison at the midpoint eliminates half the remaining possibilities.

steps.title: Maintain a search window [lo, hi]
steps.detail: Start with the whole array: lo = 0, hi = n-1. The invariant is: if the target exists, its index is somewhere in [lo, hi].

steps.title: Probe the middle
steps.detail: Compute mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2. Writing it this way (instead of (lo + hi)/2) avoids integer overflow when lo and hi are large.

steps.title: Compare and discard half
steps.detail: If a[mid] == target, you're done. If a[mid] < target, the answer must be to the right, so set lo = mid + 1. Otherwise it's to the left, so set hi = mid - 1.

steps.title: Stop when the window is empty
steps.detail: Loop while lo <= hi. When lo > hi the window is empty, meaning the target isn't present — return -1.

complexity.timeReason: Each iteration discards half the remaining window, so the number of iterations is at most ⌈log₂ n⌉.
complexity.spaceReason: Only a few integer variables (lo, hi, mid) are used. The recursive form would cost O(log n) stack space.

pitfalls: Using (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow for large indices — prefer lo + (hi - lo) / 2.
Off-by-one in the loop: 'while (lo < hi)' vs 'while (lo <= hi)' changes whether the last element is ever checked.
Forgetting the array must be sorted — binary search on unsorted data returns garbage.
Updating lo = mid (instead of mid + 1) can cause an infinite loop when the window size is 1 or 2.

dryRun.clickMoment: Notice step 1 instantly removed indices 0–4 from consideration with a single comparison. Three comparisons total located the target in a 9-element array — and it would still be only ~4 comparisons for 16 elements, ~5 for 32. That exponential shrinking is the 'aha'.

problems.title: Binary Search
problems.statement: Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target, return its index or -1 if absent.
problems.hint: This is the textbook template. Be careful with the loop condition lo <= hi and the mid + 1 / mid - 1 updates.

approach: This is the canonical template. Keep a closed window [lo, hi] that always contains the answer if it exists.
Probe the midpoint; if it equals the target you are done, otherwise the comparison tells you which half to discard. Loop while lo <= hi and return -1 when the window empties.

problems.title: First Bad Version
problems.statement: Versions 1..n; after some version all are bad. Find the first bad version using as few API calls as possible.
problems.hint: Search for a boundary, not an exact value. When isBad(mid) is true, the answer is mid or to its left, so set hi = mid.
problems.tests: Binary search on a monotonic predicate (boundary search).

approach: Here we search for a boundary, not an exact value. The predicate isBadVersion is monotonic: once it turns true it stays true.
Use the half-open style: while lo < hi, if isBadVersion(mid) the first bad version is mid or to its left (hi = mid), else it is strictly right (lo = mid + 1). lo converges on the first true.

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.statement: A sorted array was rotated at an unknown pivot. Find a target in O(log n).
problems.hint: At each mid, one half is always sorted. Decide which half is sorted, then check whether the target lies within its range to know where to go.
problems.tests: Adapting the discard rule when the array isn't globally monotonic.

approach: The array is two sorted runs. At any mid, at least one of [lo, mid] and [mid, hi] is fully sorted — compare a[lo] with a[mid] to find which.
If the left half is sorted and the target lies inside [a[lo], a[mid]), go left; symmetrically for the right half. Each step still halves the range, giving O(log n).

problems.title: Koko Eating Bananas
problems.statement: Find the minimum eating speed k so all banana piles are finished within h hours.
problems.hint: Binary search on the answer (the speed), not the array. feasible(k) is monotonic: if speed k works, so does k+1.
problems.tests: Binary search on the answer space + a feasibility predicate.

approach: Binary search on the answer (the speed k), not on the array. feasible(k) = total hours to finish all piles at speed k is monotonic: faster speed never needs more hours.
Search k in [1, max(pile)]. Hours for a pile of size x at speed k is ceil(x/k). Find the smallest k whose total hours <= h.

problems.title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
problems.statement: Given two sorted arrays, find the median of their combined elements in O(log(m+n)).
problems.hint: Binary search on the partition point of the smaller array so that left halves contain exactly half the total elements and maxLeft <= minRight.
problems.tests: Binary search over a partition with careful boundary conditions.

approach: Binary search the partition point of the smaller array. Choose i elements from A and j from B so the left side holds exactly half of all elements.
A partition is valid when maxLeft(A) <= minRight(B) and maxLeft(B) <= minRight(A). Use ±infinity sentinels at the ends; then the median is read off the boundary values. O(log min(m,n)).
